claim: Puttaswamy (p.83, para 84) quotes NALSA, Radhakrishnan J.: 'values of privacy, self-identity, autonomy and personal integrity are fundamental rights' of the transgender community (under Art 19(1)(a)). It also quotes NALSA that Article 21 protects 'one's personal autonomy, one's right to privacy'. This is the source of the question's 'privacy relating to self-identity'.
value: NALSA on privacy and self-identity, as quoted

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(H) (Chandrachud J., for four judges): an invasion of life or personal liberty must meet a three-fold test: legality (a law), need (a legitimate State aim) and proportionality (a rational nexus between object and means); procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. This is the test to apply to the 2026 amendment.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Same as topic ledger POL03-D13; repeated so the standard sits beside the amendment. Applying it to the 2026 Act is analysis, not a court finding.

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(I): privacy has a negative content (restrains the State from intruding) and a positive content that 'imposes an obligation on the state to take all necessary measures' to protect privacy.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J., on Koushal (the Section 377 case): the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons are not 'so-called' rights but 'real rights'; sexual orientation is an essential attribute of privacy, and discrimination on it offends dignity. The 2026 proviso excluding 'different sexual orientations' is the point where this reasoning would be tested.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Puttaswamy called the Koushal view unsustainable (the later Navtej Johar judgment of 6 Sep 2018 is not read here, so no claim about it).
